result.content:
### Define a class with classDef

Source: https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/blob/develop/docs/syntax/entityRelationshipDiagram.md

Defines a reusable class of styles using the classDef keyword. The example sets fill, stroke, and stroke-width for the class named className.

```text
    classDef className fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px
```

--------------------------------

### classDef styling example

Source: https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/blob/develop/docs/syntax/flowchart.md

Recommended approach to style flowchart nodes using classDef syntax. Applies fill and stroke colors to nodes with the myStyle class.

```mermaid-example
flowchart LR
    A:::myStyle --> B
    classDef myStyle fill:#ff0000,stroke:#ffff00,stroke-width:4px
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A:::myStyle --> B
    classDef myStyle fill:#ff0000,stroke:#ffff00,stroke-width:4px
```

--------------------------------

### State diagram using ::: operator to apply styles

Source: https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/blob/develop/demos/state.html

This example uses the ::: operator to apply classDef styles directly to states in transitions. It includes the same classDef definitions and shows the start and end states with styles applied.

```mermaid
stateDiagram
  direction TB

	  accTitle: This is the accessible title
      accDescr: This is an accessible description

      classDef notMoving fill:white
      classDef movement font-style:italic
      classDef badBadEvent fill:#f00,color:white,font-weight:bold,stroke-width:2px,stroke:yellow

      [*] --> Still:::notMoving
      Still --> [*]
      Still --> Moving:::movement
      Moving --> Still
      Moving --> Crash:::movement
      Crash:::badBadEvent --> [*]
```

### Links between nodes > Using classDef Statements for Animations

Source: https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/blob/develop/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/flowchart.md

### Using classDef Statements for Animations

You can also animate edges by assigning a class to them and then defining animation properties in a `classDef` statement. For example:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A e1@--> B
  classDef animate stroke-dasharray: 9,5,stroke-dashoffset: 900,animation: dash 25s linear infinite;
  class e1 animate
```

In this snippet:

- `e1@-->` creates an edge with ID `e1`.
- `classDef animate` defines a class named `animate` with styling and animation properties.
- `class e1 animate` applies the `animate` class to the edge `e1`.

**Note on Escaping Commas:**
When setting the `stroke-dasharray` property, remember to escape commas as `\,` since commas are used as delimiters in Mermaid’s style definitions.

--------------------------------

### Styling and classes > Classes

Source: https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/blob/develop/packages/mermaid/src/docs/syntax/flowchart.md

More convenient than defining the style every time is to define a class of styles and attach this class to the nodes that
should have a different look.

A class definition looks like the example below:

```
    classDef className fill:#f9f,stroke:#333,stroke-width:4px;
```

Also, it is possible to define style to multiple classes in one statement:

```
    classDef firstClassName,secondClassName font-size:12pt;
```

Attachment of a class to a node is done as per below:

```
    class nodeId1 className;
```

It is also possible to attach a class to a list of nodes in one statement:

```
    class nodeId1,nodeId2 className;
```

A shorter form of adding a class is to attach the classname to the node using the `:::`operator as per below:

```mermaid-example
flowchart LR
    A:::someclass --> B
    classDef someclass fill:#f96
```

This form can be used when declaring multiple links between nodes:

```mermaid-example
flowchart LR
    A:::foo & B:::bar --> C:::foobar
    classDef foo stroke:#f00
    classDef bar stroke:#0f0
    classDef foobar stroke:#00f
```

result.content:
# Craft floor

Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.

## Verify

Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in the batched inspection rounds, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.

- **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
- **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
- **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
- **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
- **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
- **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
- **Browser surfaces:** the parts you did not draw still carry the design. Text selection, the caret, custom scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, and the numerals in tabular data all ship with browser defaults that belong to no design system. Theme them from the palette. This is the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, and the one models skip most reliably.
- **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
- **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.

## Refuse

These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.

Page scaffolds:

- Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
- The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
- A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
- A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.

Surface habits:

- Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
- Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
- A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
- Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
- Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
- Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
- A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
- Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
- Geometric masks standing in for organic contours. A circle, polygon, or radial-gradient cutout approximating a photographic subject's edge is the cheap version of the effect and reads worse than omitting it. Derive an alpha matte from the actual image, or produce a cut-out asset.
- Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.

The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.

-# Data Flow Diagrams (DFD)
-
-## Level 0 - Payment acceptance system
-
-```mermaid
-flowchart LR
-    subgraph External Actors
-        App["Zapper App"]
-        AcmeStub["Acme Pay Stub"]
-        AcmeAdvice["Acme Payment Advice"]
-        AcmeSwitch["Acme Transaction Status"]
-    end
-
-    subgraph Core System
-        Intake["Payment Intake API"]
-        Orchestrator["Payment Orchestrator"]
-        NotificationHandler["Notification Endpoints"]
-        SummaryService["Daily Summary Reporter"]
-        RealTimeQuery["Real Time Transaction Query"]
-        PaymentAdvice["Payment Advice Endpoint (Basic Auth)"]
-        TransactionStatus["Transaction Status Webhook (HMAC)"]
-    end
-
-    subgraph Persistence
-        PaymentDB["SQL Store (Payments, History, Notifications)"]
-        TokenStore["Token/Idempotency Store"]
-    end
-
-    App -->|Payment Request| Intake
-    Intake -->|Validate + Context| Orchestrator
-    Orchestrator --> PaymentDB
-    Orchestrator -->|Submit| AcmeStub
-    AcmeStub -->|Callbacks| NotificationHandler
-    AcmeAdvice -->|Notify (Auth)| PaymentAdvice
-    AcmeSwitch -->|Webhook (HMAC)| TransactionStatus
-    PaymentAdvice --> NotificationHandler
-    TransactionStatus --> NotificationHandler
-    NotificationHandler --> PaymentDB
-    NotificationHandler --> TokenStore
-    RealTimeQuery --> PaymentDB
-    App -->|RTTQ Query| RealTimeQuery
-    SummaryService --> PaymentDB
-    TokenStore --> Orchestrator
-    SummaryService -->|Reports| App
-```
-
-## Notes
-
--- **Data stores** keep audit records and tokens separate to maintain ACID guarantees (transactions update payment + history atomically).
--- **Notification flow** always writes to a ledger-style store before emitting state changes so retries stay idempotent.
--- **Payment Advice** and **Transaction Status** endpoints enrich the same Notification Handler but have distinct authentication (basic vs. HMAC) and thus are modeled separately.
--- **Real Time Transaction Query** lets the App reconcile timed-out submissions without resubmitting, ensuring the system respects Append-only histories while remaining idempotent.
--- **Summary service** reads the same stores in a read-only fashion, following ISO/IEC 25010 reliability and performance expectations.

+## Level 0 - Payment acceptance system
+

+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'tertiaryColor': '#38bdf8', 'secondaryColor': '#fb7185', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%

+        AcmeStub["Acme Pay Stub"]:::actor

+

+# Sequence Diagrams
+
+## 1. Payment submission flow
+
+```mermaid
+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#fb7185', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
+sequenceDiagram
+    participant App as Zapper App
+    participant API as Payment Intake
+    participant Orchestrator
+    participant Acme as Acme Stub
+    participant DB as SQL Store
+
+    App->>API: Submit payment request (customer, sub-merchant, amount, app payment ID)
+    API->>Orchestrator: Validate, augment with metadata
+    Orchestrator->>DB: Begin transaction, create Payment + History
+    Orchestrator->>Acme: POST /api/payment (tokenized card, headers)
+    Acme-->>Orchestrator: Response (status, ReconID, codes)
+    Orchestrator->>DB: Commit payment update, append history
+    Orchestrator-->>App: Return correlation info + pending status
+```
+
+## 2. Notification dedup/reordering
+
+```mermaid
+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#38bdf8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
+sequenceDiagram
+    participant Acme as Acme Stub
+    participant Notify as Notification Handler
+    participant DB as SQL Store
+    participant Orchestrator
+
+    Acme->>Notify: Callback (status update)
+    Notify->>DB: Insert notification record (idempotent insert)
+    DB-->>Notify: Ack
+    Notify->>Orchestrator: Map to payment, determine new status
+    Orchestrator->>DB: Update payment state + history transactionally
+    Notify-->>Acme: 200 OK
+```
+
+## 3. Daily summary generation
+
+```mermaid
+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#f59e0b', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
+sequenceDiagram
+    participant Scheduler
+    participant Summary as Summary Service
+    participant DB as SQL Store
+    participant Client as Reporting Consumer
+
+    Scheduler->>Summary: Trigger aggregated summary for date, merchant, currency
+    Summary->>DB: Query payments grouped by status (approved, declined, reversed, refunded)
+    DB-->>Summary: Return aggregates
+    Summary->>Client: Provide daily report (counts + totals)
+```
+
+## 4. Payment Advice notification
+
+```mermaid
+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#fb7185', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
+sequenceDiagram
+    participant AcmeAdvice as Acme Payment Advice
+    participant AdviceEndpoint as Payment Advice Endpoint
+    participant NotificationSystem
+    participant DB as SQL Store
+    participant Orchestrator
+
+    AcmeAdvice->>AdviceEndpoint: POST notification (basic auth, payload)
+    AdviceEndpoint->>NotificationSystem: validate auth + envelope
+    NotificationSystem->>DB: insert notification record
+    DB-->>NotificationSystem: ack
+    NotificationSystem->>Orchestrator: apply to PaymentAggregate
+    Orchestrator->>DB: update payment + history
+    AdviceEndpoint-->>AcmeAdvice: 200 OK
+```
+
+## 5. Transaction Status webhook (Reversals/Refunds)
+
+```mermaid
+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#10b981', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
+sequenceDiagram
+    participant AcmeSwitch as Acme Transaction Status
+    participant StatusWebhook as Transaction Status Webhook
+    participant SignatureVerifier
+    participant NotificationSystem
+    participant DB as SQL Store
+
+    AcmeSwitch->>StatusWebhook: POST reversal/refund (x-signature HMAC)
+    StatusWebhook->>SignatureVerifier: validate x-signature using secret
+    SignatureVerifier-->>StatusWebhook: valid / invalid
+    StatusWebhook->>NotificationSystem: process if valid
+    NotificationSystem->>DB: append notification + history
+    StatusWebhook-->>AcmeSwitch: 200 OK (or 401 on failure)
+```
+
+## 6. Real-time transaction query
+
+```mermaid
+%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#38bdf8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
+sequenceDiagram
+    participant App as Zapper App
+    participant RTTQ as Real Time Transaction Query
+    participant DB as SQL Store
+
+    App->>RTTQ: GET /apirttq/query/Merchant/{MerchantID}?TransactionID=xxx
+    RTTQ->>DB: locate latest Payment or Notification per TransactionID/OrderNumber
+    DB-->>RTTQ: return recorded state (Processing/Success/Failure)
+    RTTQ-->>App: respond with PaymentResponse-shaped payload
+```
+
+## Notes
+
+- Each diagram is kept small so sub-components can later author their own focused diagrams when we proceed with OO design.
+- State transitions rely on idempotent inserts and transactional histories, satisfying ACID and ensuring maintainable, traceable behavior per ISO/IEC 25010.
+- Real-time queries reuse the same persistent models to avoid resubmitting timed-out requests and deliver consistent transaction status.
*** End Patch

```mermaid
    participant Acme as Acme Stub
    participant DB as SQL Store

    App->>API: Submit payment request (customer, sub-merchant, amount, app payment ID)
    API->>Orchestrator: Validate, augment with metadata
    Orchestrator->>DB: Begin transaction, create Payment + History
    Orchestrator->>Acme: POST /api/payment (tokenized card, headers)
    Acme-->>Orchestrator: Response (status, ReconID, codes)
    Orchestrator->>DB: Commit payment update, append history
    Orchestrator-->>App: Return correlation info + pending status
```

## 2. Notification dedup/reordering

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Acme as Acme Stub
    participant Notify as Notification Handler
    participant DB as SQL Store
    participant Orchestrator

    Acme->>Notify: Callback (status update)
    Notify->>DB: Insert notification record (idempotent insert)
    DB-->>Notify: Ack
    Notify->>Orchestrator: Map to payment, determine new status
    Orchestrator->>DB: Update payment state + history transactionally
    Notify-->>Acme: 200 OK
```

## 3. Daily summary generation

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Scheduler
    participant Summary as Summary Service
    participant DB as SQL Store
    participant Client as Reporting Consumer

    Scheduler->>Summary: Trigger aggregated summary for date, merchant, currency
    Summary->>DB: Query payments grouped by status (approved, declined, reversed, refunded)
    DB-->>Summary: Return aggregates
    Summary->>Client: Provide daily report (counts + totals)
```

## 4. Payment Advice notification

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant AcmeAdvice as Acme Payment Advice
    participant AdviceEndpoint as Payment Advice Endpoint
    participant NotificationSystem
    participant DB as SQL Store
    participant Orchestrator

    AcmeAdvice->>AdviceEndpoint: POST notification (basic auth, payload)
    AdviceEndpoint->>NotificationSystem: validate auth + envelope
    NotificationSystem->>DB: insert notification record
    DB-->>NotificationSystem: ack
    NotificationSystem->>Orchestrator: apply to PaymentAggregate
    Orchestrator->>DB: update payment + history
    AdviceEndpoint-->>AcmeAdvice: 200 OK
```

## 5. Transaction Status webhook (Reversals/Refunds)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant AcmeSwitch as Acme Transaction Status
    participant StatusWebhook as Transaction Status Webhook
    participant SignatureVerifier
    participant NotificationSystem
    participant DB as SQL Store

    AcmeSwitch->>StatusWebhook: POST reversal/refund (x-signature HMAC)
    StatusWebhook->>SignatureVerifier: validate x-signature using secret
    SignatureVerifier-->>StatusWebhook: valid / invalid
    StatusWebhook->>NotificationSystem: process if valid
    NotificationSystem->>DB: append notification + history
    StatusWebhook-->>AcmeSwitch: 200 OK (or 401 on failure)
```

## 6. Real-time transaction query

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Zapper App
    participant RTTQ as Real Time Transaction Query
    participant DB as SQL Store

    App->>RTTQ: GET /apirttq/query/Merchant/{MerchantID}?TransactionID=xxx
    RTTQ->>DB: locate latest Payment or Notification per TransactionID/OrderNumber

    RTTQ-->>App: respond with PaymentResponse-shaped payload
```

- Each diagram is kept small so sub-components can later author their own focused diagrams when we proceed with OO design.
- State transitions rely on idempotent inserts and transactional histories, satisfying ACID and ensuring maintainable, traceable behavior per ISO/IEC 25010.
- Real-time queries reuse the same persistent models to avoid resubmitting timed-out requests and present consistent TransactionStatus.

This skill gives you the tools and permission to create design that earns to be called out-of-distribution craft: Whereas before, your design work would have been safe, timid and measured, you now approach every design task as an award-winning design director with impeccable understanding for what makes exceptional design work: production-grade code, peak creativity, a clear POV, deep understanding of the needs of the client and users, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Go all out. No hedging, no shortcuts. The deliverable must be complete (except assets the user must provide).
- Dream big and bold. Distinct, beautiful, outstanding and highly inspiring work.
- Verify in bounded passes, not a loop, and the ceiling covers the whole cycle: screenshots, defect scans, micro-edits, and rebuilds alike. Build fully, inspect once with a batched round (desktop and mobile together on the web; the shipped device classes on a native platform), fix everything it shows in one batch, confirm with at most one more round, and stop polishing. Open-ended self-QA burns the user's money doing worse what the finish handoffs do better.

## Setup

1. Run `<skill-base-dir>/scripts/impeccable context` once per session, where `<skill-base-dir>` is the directory that contains this SKILL.md (the skill folder, not a plugin root two levels above it); keep cwd at the user's project. That base directory resolves every `.github/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable <verb>` command in this skill and its references, and `.github/skills/impeccable/scripts` is the fallback only when the runtime reports no base directory. On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.github/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. It loads PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, the matching surface brief, and native-platform guidance when applicable; follow its directives and do not rerun it.
2. Load the request's playbook: its Commands-table reference for an explicit/implied sub-command, or [reference/new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for a new surface or replacement visual world. Inspect target and incumbent visual truth before editing. When the app cannot run, start with committed visual-regression goldens or screenshot fixtures; verify target and freshness against current tokens, CSS, components, or assets, resolve conflicts, and compare theme/variant captures.
3. After resolving analysis and direction, read [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, including small refinements. It carries the quality floor, the absolute bans, and the reflexes no detector catches. Do not load it for planning-only work.

**Launcher unavailable:** On refusal or failure, send a separate message **before the next tool call**: “Context loading did not run; I’ll read the existing project context directly.” Then read existing PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md without inventing missing context, follow applicable steps 2–3, and continue through permitted tools. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. See [new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for new surfaces and [operate.md](reference/operate.md) for deeper Operate/Read guidance.

# Sequence Diagrams

## 1. Payment submission flow

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#fb7185', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Zapper App
    participant API as Payment Intake
    participant Orchestrator
    participant Acme as Acme Stub
    participant DB as SQL Store

    App->>API: Submit payment request (customer, sub-merchant, amount, app payment ID)
    API->>Orchestrator: Validate, augment with metadata
    Orchestrator->>DB: Begin transaction, create Payment + History
    Orchestrator->>Acme: POST /api/payment (tokenized card, headers)
    Acme-->>Orchestrator: Response (status, ReconID, codes)
    Orchestrator->>DB: Commit payment update, append history
    Orchestrator-->>App: Return correlation info + pending status
```

## 2. Notification dedup/reordering

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#38bdf8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    participant Acme as Acme Stub
    participant Notify as Notification Handler
    participant DB as SQL Store
    participant Orchestrator

    Acme->>Notify: Callback (status update)
    Notify->>DB: Insert notification record (idempotent insert)
    DB-->>Notify: Ack
    Notify->>Orchestrator: Map to payment, determine new status
    Orchestrator->>DB: Update payment state + history transactionally
    Notify-->>Acme: 200 OK
```

## 3. Daily summary generation

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#f59e0b', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    participant Scheduler
    participant Summary as Summary Service
    participant DB as SQL Store
    participant Client as Reporting Consumer

    Scheduler->>Summary: Trigger aggregated summary for date, merchant, currency
    Summary->>DB: Query payments grouped by status (approved, declined, reversed, refunded)
    DB-->>Summary: Return aggregates
    Summary->>Client: Provide daily report (counts + totals)
```

## 4. Payment Advice notification

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#fb7185', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    participant AcmeAdvice as Acme Payment Advice
    participant AdviceEndpoint as Payment Advice Endpoint
    participant NotificationSystem
    participant DB as SQL Store
    participant Orchestrator

    AcmeAdvice->>AdviceEndpoint: POST notification (basic auth, payload)
    AdviceEndpoint->>NotificationSystem: validate auth + envelope
    NotificationSystem->>DB: insert notification record
    DB-->>NotificationSystem: ack
    NotificationSystem->>Orchestrator: apply to PaymentAggregate
    Orchestrator->>DB: update payment + history
    AdviceEndpoint-->>AcmeAdvice: 200 OK
```

## 5. Transaction Status webhook (Reversals/Refunds)

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#10b981', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    participant AcmeSwitch as Acme Transaction Status
    participant StatusWebhook as Transaction Status Webhook
    participant SignatureVerifier
    participant NotificationSystem
    participant DB as SQL Store

    AcmeSwitch->>StatusWebhook: POST reversal/refund (x-signature HMAC)
    StatusWebhook->>SignatureVerifier: validate x-signature using secret
    SignatureVerifier-->>StatusWebhook: valid / invalid
    StatusWebhook->>NotificationSystem: process if valid
    NotificationSystem->>DB: append notification + history
    StatusWebhook-->>AcmeSwitch: 200 OK (or 401 on failure)
```

## 6. Real-time transaction query

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#38bdf8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Zapper App
    participant RTTQ as Real Time Transaction Query
    participant DB as SQL Store

    App->>RTTQ: GET /apirttq/query/Merchant/{MerchantID}?TransactionID=xxx
    RTTQ->>DB: locate latest Payment or Notification per TransactionID/OrderNumber
    DB-->>RTTQ: return recorded state (Processing/Success/Failure)
    RTTQ-->>App: respond with PaymentResponse-shaped payload
```

## Notes

- Each diagram is kept small so sub-components can later author their own focused diagrams when we proceed with OO design.
- State transitions rely on idempotent inserts and transactional histories, satisfying ACID and ensuring maintainable, traceable behavior per ISO/IEC 25010.
- Real-time queries reuse the same persistent models to avoid resubmitting timed-out requests and present consistent TransactionStatus.
- All sequence diagrams share the same base theme (Inter font, muted edges, deliberate accent colors) so the flow of time appears cohesive across payment, notification, and reporting scenarios.

## Level 0 - Payment acceptance system

```mermaid

        Intake["Payment Intake API"]:::core

    end

    subgraph Persistence
        PaymentDB["SQL Store (Payments, History, Notifications)"]:::data
        TokenStore["Token/Idempotency Store"]:::data
    end

    App -->|Payment Request| Intake
    Intake -->|Validate + Context| Orchestrator

    Orchestrator -->|Submit| AcmeStub

    SummaryService --> PaymentDB

    classDef data fill:#219ebc,stroke:#023047,stroke-width:2px,color:#ffffff,font-weight:600;
```

- **Summary service** reads the shared stores in a read-only fashion, keeping ISO/IEC 25010 reliability and performance expectations in focus.

# Object-Oriented Analysis & Design (Phase 2)

Phase 1 gave us the DFDs, ERDs, and sequence diagrams that expose the major flows: payment submissions, notification handling, and daily reporting. Phase 2 now translates those flows into domain-aligned objects, services, and collaborators while staying stack-agnostic. We continue to honor the principles captured in `Soul.md` (ISO/IEC 25010 quality goals and ACID/SOLID/DRY/12-Factor commitments) while preparing for later adaptive refinements.

## Domain services and responsibilities

1. **Payment processing module**  
   - Intake point is `PaymentIntakeAPI` (controller/handler) responsible for validating the payload and correlating the App payment ID.
   - `PaymentOrchestrator` acts as the use-case runner: it instantiates `PaymentAggregate` state, coordinates writes to `PaymentRepository` and `PaymentHistoryRepository`, and dispatches the Acme request through `AcmeGatewayClient`.
   - `PaymentAggregate` encapsulates the payment state machine (Pending → Approved/Declined → Reversed/Refunded) and exposes commands such as `markApproved()`, `applyNotification()`, and `recordFailure()`, enforcing invariants (SOLID Single Responsibility, encapsulated behaviors).
   - `TokenStore` provides idempotent token lookups, and `IdempotencyGuard` (possibly part of the repository layer) ensures replayed requests reuse existing aggregate state.

2. **Notification handling module**  
   - `NotificationHandler` validates the incoming envelope, authenticates Acme (HMAC/Basic auth), and persists the raw payload through `NotificationRepository`.
   - `NotificationDeduplicator` interprets `AcmeMessageID` and `TransactionID` to short-circuit duplicates before state changes are applied.

**When to use this tool:**

- Requirements are ambiguous and you need specific, structured input to resolve them
- You want to collect several related preferences at once rather than asking one at a time

**Choosing field types:**
- **Enum** — when you know likely options (e.g., database engine, auth strategy, log level). The user can still provide a freeform answer. If values are identifiers (snake_case, codes), provide labels via `oneOf: [{const, title}]` so the form is readable.
- **Boolean** — for yes/no decisions (e.g., "enable caching?", "run migrations?")
- **Multi-select array** — when the user may pick any number of values from a known set (e.g., which features to include, which platforms to target). If item values are not human-readable, use `items.anyOf: [{const, title}]` instead of `items.enum`.
- **Number/integer** — for numeric-style configuration (e.g., port, timeout, retry count). The user may still enter freeform text.
- **String** — when the answer is open-ended (e.g., project name, custom path). String answers have no length, pattern, or format restrictions.

**Guidelines:**
- Keep forms focused on one topic — don't mix unrelated questions in a single form
- Provide clear `title` and `description` on each field so the user understands what they're choosing
- Set sensible `default` values when a reasonable default exists — if you recommend a specific option, make it the default
- A single-field form is perfectly fine for a simple yes/no or single choice
- Order `properties` keys in the same sequence you discuss the topics in `message` — the form renders fields in property order, so matching the description avoids forcing the user to jump around

**Example — simple single-choice question:**
```json
{
  "message": "What database should I use?",
  "requestedSchema": {
    "properties": {
      "database": {
        "type": "string",
        "title": "Database engine",
        "enum": ["PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "SQLite"],
        "default": "PostgreSQL"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**User actions:**
- The user may **accept** the form (you receive their field values)
- The user may **decline** (they chose not to answer — respect this and proceed with reasonable defaults)
- The user may **cancel** (they want to abort the current interaction)

**When to STOP and ask (do not assume):**
- Design decisions that significantly affect implementation approach
- Behavioral questions (e.g., "should this be unlimited or capped?")

## Platform prerequisites

1. **Install nvm and Node 24**
   ```bash
   curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.8/install.sh | bash
   source "$HOME/.nvm/nvm.sh"
   nvm install 24
   node -v    # should read v24.21.0
   npm -v     # should read 11.19.0
   ```

2. **Install Copilot CLI (BYOM/BYOK aware)**
   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
   ```
   After installation, run `copilot` in this repo, use `/init`, and `exit` once initialization completes. Configure BYOM/BYOK credentials via `copilot config set cloud.byoKey <FILE>` or the dashboard-provided secret so that the CLI always uses our chosen model and avoids unbounded token usage.

3. **Optional tooling that keeps us agentic**
   - **Astral UV package manager (Linux)**  
     `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh`
   - **Graphify (for structure-aware diagrams)**  
     `uv tool install graphifyy` (then run `graphifyy` from the repo as needed).
   - **Context7 (context-first guidance for autocoding)**  
     `npx ctx7 setup`
   - **Impeccable (quality guardrails and visual QA)**  
     `npm install -g impeccable` or add to devDependencies; run `impeccable scan` during reviews.

- **Copilot CLI** will be our primary agent. Keep it context aware by starting each session from this repo, pointing it at our BYOM/BYOK endpoint, and supplying only the files that describe the current focus.

- **Impeccable** runs infrequently but as a sanity check when touching UI or UX-related outputs (storyboards, instructions, or diagrams).

## Repository setup

1. `npm install` (if package files appear) or run the repo-specific bootstrap.
2. Keep environment variables in a `.env.local` (excluded) and reference them via `process.env`.
3. After tooling is ready, run `npx ctx7 validate` (if available) to check context captures before letting Copilot act.

This project is guided by a principles-first architect’s soul.

## What we want (ISO/IEC 25010 – 2023 focus)
- **Functional suitability**: every endpoint must deliver the precise payment/note/summary payloads defined in the brief.
- **Reliability & availability**: idempotent writes, durable notifications, and self-healing Acme interactions keep the service predictable even when callbacks reorder or duplicate.
- **Performance efficiency & maintainability**: modular components, bounded data flows, and observable contracts ensure the system performs without eroding clarity.
- **Security & compatibility**: message envelopes, authenticated callbacks, and environment-driven configuration all keep the system aligned with the standard.

## How we achieve it
- **ACID**: every payment+history change is in a single transaction, with notification insertions layered so retries never leave inconsistent states.
- **SOLID**: future design splits responsibilities—Payment Intake, Notification Handler, and Summary Reporter become separate services or classes with well-defined interfaces, enabling easy extension.
- **DRY**: shared logic (envelopes, header parsing, retry scaffolding) lives in reusable helpers or middleware rather than duplicated across handlers.
- **12-Factor principles**: configuration via env vars, stateless service layer backed by durable storage, logs streamed through a diagnostics module, separate dev/prod dependencies, and clean container lifecycle handling.

## ❌ Without Context7

LLMs rely on outdated or generic information about the libraries you use. You get:

- ❌ Code examples are outdated and based on year-old training data
- ❌ Hallucinated APIs that don't even exist
- ❌ Generic answers for old package versions

## ✅ With Context7

Context7 pulls up-to-date, version-specific documentation and code examples straight from the source — and places them directly into your prompt.

```txt
Create a Next.js middleware that checks for a valid JWT in cookies
and redirects unauthenticated users to `/login`. use context7
```

```txt
Configure a Cloudflare Worker script to cache
JSON API responses for five minutes. use context7
```

```txt
Show me the Supabase auth API for email/password sign-up.
```

Context7 fetches up-to-date code examples and documentation right into your LLM's context. No tab-switching, no hallucinated APIs that don't exist, no outdated code generation.

Works in two modes:

- **CLI + Skills** — installs a skill that guides your agent to fetch docs using `ctx7` CLI commands (no MCP required)
- **MCP** — registers a Context7 MCP server so your agent can call documentation tools natively

## Installation

> [!NOTE]
> **API Key Recommended**: Get a free API key at [context7.com/dashboard](https://context7.com/dashboard) for higher rate limits.

Set up Context7 for your coding agents with a single command. The `ctx7` CLI requires Node.js 18 or newer.

```bash
npx ctx7 setup
```

Authenticates via OAuth, generates an API key, and installs the appropriate skill. You can choose between CLI + Skills or MCP mode. Use `--cursor`, `--claude`, or `--opencode` to target a specific agent.

To remove the generated setup later, run `npx ctx7 remove`. If you globally installed the CLI with `npm install -g ctx7`, remove that package separately with `npm uninstall -g ctx7`.

To configure manually, use the Context7 server URL `https://mcp.context7.com/mcp` with your MCP client and pass your API key via the `Authorization: ****** header. See the link below for client-specific setup instructions.

**[Manual Installation / Other Clients →](https://context7.com/docs/resources/all-clients)**

## Important Tips

### Use Library Id

If you already know exactly which library you want to use, add its Context7 ID to your prompt. That way, Context7 can skip the library-matching step and directly retrieve docs.

```txt
Implement basic authentication with Supabase. use library /supabase/supabase for API and docs.
```

The slash syntax tells Context7 exactly which library to load docs for.

### Specify a Version

To get documentation for a specific library version, just mention the version in your prompt:

```txt
How do I set up Next.js 14 middleware? use context7
```

Context7 will automatically match the appropriate version.

### Add a Rule

If you installed via `ctx7 setup`, a skill is configured automatically that triggers Context7 for library-related questions. To set up a rule manually instead, add one to your coding agent:

- **Cursor**: `Cursor Settings > Rules`
- **Claude Code**: `CLAUDE.md`
- Or the equivalent in your coding agent

**Example rule:**

```txt
Always use Context7 when I need library/API documentation, code generation, setup or configuration steps without me having to explicitly ask.
```

- `ctx7 library <name> <query>`: Searches the Context7 index by library name and returns matching libraries with their IDs.

This skill gives you the tools and permission to create design that earns to be called out-of-distribution craft: Whereas before, your design work would have been safe, timid and measured, you now approach every design task as an award-winning design director with impeccable understanding for what makes exceptional design work: production-grade code, peak creativity, a clear POV, deep understanding of the needs of the client and users, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Go all out. No hedging, no shortcuts. The deliverable must be complete (except assets the user must provide).
- Dream big and bold. Distinct, beautiful, outstanding and highly inspiring work.
- Verify in bounded passes, not a loop, and the ceiling covers the whole cycle: screenshots, defect scans, micro-edits, and rebuilds alike. Build fully, inspect once with a batched round (desktop and mobile together on the web; the shipped device classes on a native platform), fix everything it shows in one batch, confirm with at most one more round, and stop polishing. Open-ended self-QA burns the user's money doing worse what the finish handoffs do better.

On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.github/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. You are the GitHub Copilot CLI, a terminal assistant built by GitHub. You are an interactive tool that helps users with software engineering tasks.

# Tone and style
* Lead with the outcome/main result; then explain the meaningful change and most important supporting detail. Mention a next step only when necessary, then stop—no recap, optional extras, offer to continue, or follow-up question.
* Use concise, information-dense prose; don't repeat the request or narrate obvious process.
* Match detail to the work: stay terse for simple confirmations, but explain fixes, investigations, tradeoffs, and real uncertainty. Do all needed validation, but mention validation/tests/checks only when explicitly requested.
* State incomplete, uncertain, or blocked work plainly instead of first claiming completion.
* Use GitHub-flavored Markdown and the shortest complete format—usually 1-2 paragraphs, not sections—with **bold** for labels/emphasis and blank lines between paragraphs.
* Use lists sparingly and only when genuinely easier to scan than prose; consider merging small items, never nest lists, and number only as `1. 2. 3.`. Consider a table instead of bullets with inline labels.
* Sound collaborative, direct, and natural, like a concise teammate handoff.

# Search and delegation
* Give sub-agents comprehensive context; response-brevity rules do not apply to their prompts.
* Search files/text only in the cwd or its descendants unless absolutely necessary. For code, prefer: available code intelligence > available LSP > glob > rg with a glob > bash.

# Tool usage efficiency
CRITICAL: Maximize tool efficiency:
* For simple searches, reads, or edits requiring only 2–5 direct calls, use rg, glob, view, apply_patch yourself; delegate only complex/long work that benefits from separate context, since sub-agents add latency.
* **USE PARALLEL TOOL CALLING** - when you need to perform multiple independent operations, make ALL tool calls in a SINGLE response. For example, if you need to read 3 files, make 3 view tool calls in one response, NOT 3 sequential responses.
* Chain related bash commands with && instead of separate calls
* Suppress verbose output (use --quiet, --no-pager, pipe to grep/head when appropriate)
* Batching does not replace investigation; take as many turns as needed to understand before acting.
* Default task agents to sync; use background only while doing independent work, not to poll while idle.

<rules_for_code_changes>
* Make precise, complete, surgical changes that fully address the request; prefer completeness over a minimal but incomplete fix, and avoid unrelated changes.
* Don't fix unrelated pre-existing issues, but do fix bugs caused by or tightly coupled to your changes.
* Update directly related documentation.
* Validate that your changes preserve existing behavior
* Prioritize correctness, clarity, and reliability over speed. Fix the root cause/core ask; avoid risky shortcuts, speculation, and hacks.

result.content:
# Craft floor

Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.

## Verify

Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in the batched inspection rounds, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.

- **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
- **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
- **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
- **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
- **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
- **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
- **Browser surfaces:** the parts you did not draw still carry the design. Text selection, the caret, custom scrollbars, focus rings, underline offset, and the numerals in tabular data all ship with browser defaults that belong to no design system. Theme them from the palette. This is the cheapest signal that a page was built rather than assembled, and the one models skip most reliably.
- **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
- **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.

## Refuse

These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.

Page scaffolds:

- Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
- The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
- A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
- A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.

Surface habits:

- Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
- Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
- A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
- Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
- Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
- Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
- A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
- Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
- Geometric masks standing in for organic contours. A circle, polygon, or radial-gradient cutout approximating a photographic subject's edge is the cheap version of the effect and reads worse than omitting it. Derive an alpha matte from the actual image, or produce a cut-out asset.
- Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.

The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.

result.content:
# Structured Systems Analysis & Design Phase

This phase remains deliberately stack-agnostic. We are exploring the problem space through data flows, entities, and interactions before selecting languages, frameworks, or an architectural stance. The goal is a modular, high-level design made of independent components that can later be mapped to OO or adaptive patterns.

## Phase deliverables

- **DFD** describing how payments, notification callbacks (payment advice + transaction status), real-time transaction queries, and summaries move through the system and its supporting data stores. _(See [DFD](./dfd.md))_
- **ERD** capturing the persistent model for merchants, cards, payments, and history. _(See [ERD](./erd.md))_
- **Sequence diagrams** that show the lifecycle of a payment request, notifications (including the payment advice webhook and the transaction status webhook), real-time transaction queries, and the daily summary generation. _(See [Sequence diagrams](./sequence.md))_

## High-level component overview

1. **External interfaces**
   - **Payment Intake API**: accepts customer, sub-merchant, and amount. Responsible for request correlation and validation.
   - **Notification endpoints**: publicly reachable handlers that authenticate Acme callbacks, deduplicate, and emit state transitions.
   - **Summary/reporting surface**: exposes per-merchant daily summaries either via API or query.
2. **Core coordination**
   - **Payment orchestration**: builds Acme request, records intent, updates payment status, and surfaces diagnostics.
   - **Acme stub**: imitates the payment gateway with configurable delays, reordering, and idempotency safeguards.
   - **Durable persistence**: applies ACID principles, stores audit trails, and ensures notifications land in a consistent, append-only ledger.
   - **Real Time Transaction Query service**: exposes the `/apirttq/query` pattern so the service can reconcile timed-out submissions and keep outcomes consistent.

3. **Supporting services**
   - **Idempotency/token store** for ensuring retries are safe.
   - **Diagnostics/logging module** that captures correlation IDs, message headers, and environment context for troubleshooting.

## Compliance & guiding constraints

This analysis already keeps ISO/IEC 25010 quality attributes top-of-mind (functional suitability, reliability, performance efficiency, security, maintainability, etc.). The resulting architecture must be extendable into SOLID/DRY responsibilities once we choose a stack, and remain compatible with 12-Factor deployment targets.

The Notification subsystem also covers both **Payment Advice** (basic auth) and **Transaction Status webhooks** (HMAC signatures + retries) so replayed or out-of-order updates stay idempotent. The diagrams now use a coherent style guide derived from Context7-sourced Mermaid class definitions so colors, fonts, and accents reinforce the roles and data paths.

For the next phase we will do Object Oriented analysis and design, referencing these artifacts to derive classes, interfaces, and adapters before validating with an adaptive design approach. The working area for that transition is documented in `docs/design/README.md`.

# Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD)

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'secondaryColor': '#fb7185', 'tertiaryColor': '#0ea5e9', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'nodeBorder': '#94a3b8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%
erDiagram
    SUBMERCHANT {
        string SubMerchantID PK "Zapper identifier"
        string TradingName
        string City
        string Region
        string Country
        string MerchantCategoryCode
        string CardAcceptorName
    }

    CUSTOMER {
        string CustomerID PK
        string Email
    }

    STORED_CARD {
        string Token PK
        string CustomerID FK
        string Email
        string CardOnFileScenario
    }

    PAYMENT {
        string PaymentID PK
        string AppPaymentID
        string CustomerID FK
        string SubMerchantID FK
        long Amount
        string CurrencyCode
        string TransactionStatus
        string Channel
        datetime CreatedAt
        datetime UpdatedAt
    }

    PAYMENT_HISTORY {
        string HistoryID PK
        string PaymentID FK
        string EventType
        string Details
        datetime OccurredAt
    }

    NOTIFICATION {
        string NotificationID PK
        string PaymentID FK
        string AcmeMessageID
        string TransactionStatus
        string ResponseCode
        string RawPayload
        datetime ReceivedAt
    }

    PAYMENT ||--|{ PAYMENT_HISTORY : records
    PAYMENT ||--|{ NOTIFICATION : influenced_by
    CUSTOMER ||--|{ STORED_CARD : owns
    CUSTOMER ||--|{ PAYMENT : initiates
    SUBMERCHANT ||--|{ PAYMENT : receives
    STORED_CARD }|..|| CUSTOMER : "references"
    classDef entity fill: #fcd34d,stroke:#be123c,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,font-weight:600;
    classDef audit fill:#bae6fd,stroke:#1d4ed8,stroke-width:2px,color:#0f172a,font-weight:500;
    class SUBMERCHANT,CUSTOMER,STORED_CARD entity
    class PAYMENT entity
    class PAYMENT_HISTORY,NOTIFICATION audit
```

## Notes

- Every write to `PAYMENT` pairs with a `PAYMENT_HISTORY` entry to satisfy audit and ACID requirements; the colored class legend separates operational tables from auditing tables.
- Notifications live in their own table so retries accumulate without mutating prior rows, supporting the ISO/IEC 25010 reliability expectation.
- This schema remains intentionally minimal to keep the analysis phase stack-independent while still highlighting normalization and indexing for the next iterations.


## 2. Notification dedup/reordering

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#38bdf8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%

    participant Notify as Notification\nHandler
    participant DB as SQL\nStore
    participant Orchestrator

    Notify->>DB: Insert notification record (idempotent insert)
    DB-->>Notify: Ack
    Notify->>Orchestrator: Map to payment, determine new status
    Orchestrator->>DB: Update payment state + history transactionally
    Notify-->>Acme: 200 OK
```

## 3. Daily summary generation

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#f59e0b', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%

    participant Summary as Summary\nService
    participant DB as SQL\nStore
    participant Client as Reporting\nConsumer

    Scheduler->>Summary: Trigger aggregated summary for date, merchant, currency
    Summary->>DB: Query payments grouped by status (approved, declined, reversed, refunded)
    DB-->>Summary: Return aggregates
    Summary->>Client: Provide daily report (counts + totals)
```

## 4. Payment Advice notification

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#fb7185', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%

    participant AcmeAdvice as Acme Payment\nAdvice

    participant NotificationSystem
    participant DB as SQL\nStore

    AdviceEndpoint->>NotificationSystem: validate auth + envelope
    NotificationSystem->>DB: insert notification record
    DB-->>NotificationSystem: ack
    NotificationSystem->>Orchestrator: apply to PaymentAggregate
    Orchestrator->>DB: update payment + history
    AdviceEndpoint-->>AcmeAdvice: 200 OK
```

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#10b981', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%

    participant AcmeSwitch as Acme Transaction\nStatus
    participant StatusWebhook as Transaction Status\nWebhook
    participant SignatureVerifier
    participant NotificationSystem
    participant DB as SQL\nStore

    AcmeSwitch->>StatusWebhook: POST reversal/refund (x-signature HMAC)
    StatusWebhook->>SignatureVerifier: validate x-signature using secret
    SignatureVerifier-->>StatusWebhook: valid / invalid
    StatusWebhook->>NotificationSystem: process if valid
    NotificationSystem->>DB: append notification + history
    StatusWebhook-->>AcmeSwitch: 200 OK (or 401 on failure)
```

## 6. Real-time transaction query

```mermaid
%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#0f172a', 'edgeLabelBackground': '#e0f2fe', 'sequenceNumberColor': '#38bdf8', 'fontFamily': 'Inter, system-ui, sans-serif'}}}%%

    participant App as Zapper\nApp
    participant RTTQ as Real Time\nTransaction Query

```

- Each diagram is kept small so sub-components can later author their own focused diagrams when we proceed with OO design.

# Object-Oriented Analysis & Design (Phase 2)

Phase 1 gave us the DFDs, ERDs, and sequence diagrams that expose the major flows: payment submissions, notification handling, and daily reporting. Phase 2 now translates those flows into domain-aligned objects, services, and collaborators while staying stack-agnostic. We continue to honor the principles captured in `Soul.md` (ISO/IEC 25010 quality goals and ACID/SOLID/DRY/12-Factor commitments) while preparing for later adaptive refinements. Every diagram uses the Context7-sourced Mermaid theme so colors, contrast, and typography stay cohesive across the analysis artifacts.

## Domain services and responsibilities

1. **Payment processing module**  
   - Intake point is `PaymentIntakeAPI` (controller/handler) responsible for validating the payload and correlating the App payment ID.
   - `PaymentOrchestrator` acts as the use-case runner: it instantiates `PaymentAggregate` state, coordinates writes to `PaymentRepository` and `PaymentHistoryRepository`, and dispatches the Acme request through `AcmeGatewayClient`.
   - `PaymentAggregate` encapsulates the payment state machine (Pending → Approved/Declined → Reversed/Refunded) and exposes commands such as `markApproved()`, `applyNotification()`, and `recordFailure()`, enforcing invariants (SOLID Single Responsibility, encapsulated behaviors).
   - `TokenStore` provides idempotent token lookups, and `IdempotencyGuard` (possibly part of the repository layer) ensures replayed requests reuse existing aggregate state.

2. **Notification handling module**  
   - `NotificationHandler` validates the incoming envelope, authenticates Acme (HMAC/Basic auth), and persists the raw payload through `NotificationRepository`.
   - `NotificationDeduplicator` interprets `AcmeMessageID` and `TransactionID` to short-circuit duplicates before state changes are applied.
   - `PaymentStateTransitionService` orbits the `PaymentAggregate`, applying updates transactionally and emitting `PaymentHistory` entries for auditability.
   - Observers/listeners (e.g., `DiagnosticsPublisher`) can capture correlation IDs and diagnostics metadata at each transition.

3. **Summary/reporting module**  
   - `SummaryScheduler` or a cron trigger drives `DailySummaryService`.
   - `DailySummaryService` queries aggregated views (e.g., using `SummaryQueryBuilder`) to fetch counts/totals per sub-merchant and currency, respecting the `Payment` statuses.
   - `DailySummaryPresenter` optionally renders API responses or exports structured JSON/CSV while ensuring calculations are deterministic (12-Factor reprensentations, e.g., environment-driven timezone).

4. **Infrastructure/utility layer**  
   - `Configurations` are provided via environment-backed factories (12-Factor Config).  
   - `AcmeGatewayClient` wraps HTTP calls with concurrency management (circuit breakers/throttling) and ensures any `HttpClient` or `SqlConnection` is shared or pooled.
   - `DiagnosticsLogger` records results per ISO/IEC 25010 reliability, emitting structured logs and metrics for tracing.
5. **Supporting entry points**
   - `RealTimeTransactionQueryService` surfaces the `/apirttq/query` endpoint so the App can reconcile timed-out requests without resubmitting.
   - `PaymentAdviceHandler` and `TransactionStatusWebhookHandler` are specialized `NotificationHandler` implementations that enforce the correct authentication (basic vs. HMAC) before delegating to the shared notification flow.

## Object-oriented diagrams

- [Payment domain classes](./payment-domain-classes.md)
- [Notification domain classes](./notification-domain-classes.md)
- [Summary domain classes](./summary-domain-classes.md)

Each diagram is intentionally focused on a component so we can extend, validate, and iterate (Phase 3 adaptive design) without inflating a single file. They also expose the hooks required for later dependency injection, composition, testing, and SOLID-friendly refactors.

```mermaid

        +beginTransaction()
    }

    class PaymentHistoryRepository {
        +appendHistory(string paymentId, string eventType, string details)
    }

    class AcmeGatewayClient {
        +submitPayment(AcmePaymentPayload payload)
        +configureTimeouts()
    }

    class TokenStore {
        +findToken(string customerId)
        +storeToken(string token, string customerId)
    }

    class RealTimeTransactionQueryService {
        +queryByTransactionId(string transactionId)
        +queryByOrderNumber(string orderNumber)
    }
```

- `RealTimeTransactionQueryService` reuses the same repositories to answer `/apirttq/query` lookups and prevents duplicate submissions resulting from timed-out calls.
- `TokenStore` is an injected dependency that can be swapped for a caching tier or a shared SQL table; this keeps the design open for future scaling.
- Controllers, services, repositories, and support components are deliberately color-coded via Mermaid `classDef` styling so the diagrams remain legible when we export them for reviews or embed them in the final solution doc.

# Adaptive Analysis & Design (Phase 3)

Phase 3 bridges the stack-agnostic OO model into an implementation blueprint through iterative validation and incremental refinement. This layer of work keeps all previously captured artifacts relevant, while ensuring each component can be safely realized with concrete technologies that preserve our guiding principles (ISO/IEC 25010, ACID, SOLID, DRY, 12-Factor).

## Goals for this phase

1. **Technology mapping** – for each domain service (payment, notification, summary) confirm the concrete frameworks, libraries, and deployment targets we will use. The mapping documents how we will:
   - Persist the ERD entities with SQL migrations and ORM/data access layers.
   - Implement the DFD flows using async APIs, background workers, or pub/sub if needed.
   - Tie the sequence diagrams into endpoint contracts, retry policies, and authentication requirements (Acme Payment Advice Basic Auth, Transaction Status webhook HMAC validation, Real Time Transaction Query).
2. **Resilience tuning** – specify how the adaptive design handles timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and backpressure by:
   - Defining invariants for `PaymentAggregate` so state transitions stay consistent under duplicate or out-of-order notifications.
   - Ensuring `AcmeGatewayClient` can be swapped between stubbed and live deployments while conserving instrumentation for diagnostics.
   - Guaranteeing the Notification subsystem acknowledges each delivery (200 on success, 401/400 on invalid auth or signature) and replays the exact payload when Acme retries after failures.
3. **Instrumentation & compliance checks** – choose logging/metrics/health checks that confirm observability expectations from ISO/IEC 25010 and 12-Factor. This includes:
   - Emitting structured logs for every payment lifecycle event.
   - Exposing health/readiness endpoints and hooking them into diagnostics modules already outlined in `docs/analysis/structured-systems-analysis.md`.
4. **Iterative validation** – define a lightweight validation loop that cycles through:
   - Reviewing each Mermaid diagram for consistency with the chosen stack.
   - Confirming ACID-enforcing transactions exist (e.g., via pseudo-SQL or migration snippets).
   - Planning safety nets (idempotency, deduplication, telemetry) before coding.

## Outputs

- ✅ A refined implementation plan showing how each class/repository ties to the chosen .NET 8 stack, container configuration, and SQL persistence strategy.
- ✅ Documented trade-offs for scaling and observability, ensuring the adaptive approach stays flexible (e.g., injecting alternate storage for the token store, instrumenting Summary Scheduler to avoid load spikes).
- ✅ A checklist for the next sprint that ensures the structured analysis artifacts remain the source of truth as we start coding.

Phase 3 is the final preparatory layer before implementation: it converts our abstract models into runnable modules while honoring the quality, reliability, and operational commitments in `Soul.md`.

# Structured Systems Analysis & Design Phase

This phase remains deliberately stack-agnostic. We are exploring the problem space through data flows, entities, and interactions before selecting languages, frameworks, or an architectural stance. The goal is a modular, high-level design made of independent components that can later be mapped to OO or adaptive patterns.

## Phase deliverables

- **DFD** describing how payments, notification callbacks (payment advice + transaction status), real-time transaction queries, and summaries move through the system and its supporting data stores. _(See [DFD](./dfd.md))_
- **ERD** capturing the persistent model for merchants, cards, payments, and history. _(See [ERD](./erd.md))_
- **Sequence diagrams** that show the lifecycle of a payment request, notifications (including the payment advice webhook and the transaction status webhook), real-time transaction queries, and the daily summary generation. _(See [Sequence diagrams](./sequence.md))_

## High-level component overview

1. **External interfaces**
   - **Payment Intake API**: accepts customer, sub-merchant, and amount. Responsible for request correlation and validation.
   - **Notification endpoints**: publicly reachable handlers that authenticate Acme callbacks, deduplicate, and emit state transitions.
   - **Summary/reporting surface**: exposes per-merchant daily summaries either via API or query.
2. **Core coordination**
   - **Payment orchestration**: builds Acme request, records intent, updates payment status, and surfaces diagnostics.
   - **Acme stub**: imitates the payment gateway with configurable delays, reordering, and idempotency safeguards.
   - **Durable persistence**: applies ACID principles, stores audit trails, and ensures notifications land in a consistent, append-only ledger.
   - **Real Time Transaction Query service**: exposes the `/apirttq/query` pattern so the service can reconcile timed-out submissions and keep outcomes consistent.

3. **Supporting services**
   - **Idempotency/token store** for ensuring retries are safe.
   - **Diagnostics/logging module** that captures correlation IDs, message headers, and environment context for troubleshooting.

## Compliance & guiding constraints

This analysis already keeps ISO/IEC 25010 quality attributes top-of-mind (functional suitability, reliability, performance efficiency, security, maintainability, etc.). The resulting architecture must be extendable into SOLID/DRY responsibilities once we choose a stack, and remain compatible with 12-Factor deployment targets.

The Notification subsystem also covers both **Payment Advice** (basic auth) and **Transaction Status webhooks** (HMAC signatures + retries) so replayed or out-of-order updates stay idempotent. The diagrams now use a coherent style guide derived from Context7-sourced Mermaid class definitions so colors, fonts, and accents reinforce the roles and data paths.

For the next phase we will do Object Oriented analysis and design, referencing these artifacts to derive classes, interfaces, and adapters before validating with an adaptive design approach. The working area for that transition is documented in `docs/design/README.md`.
